title: Tencent Leases 100,000 Oracle AI Chips for $7B as Chinese State Lenders Finance Banned Nvidia Hardware
subhead: A $7 billion lease lets Tencent tap 100,000 advanced AI chips through Southeast Asian data centers, while a Bloomberg report reveals Chinese state-backed financing for export-restricted Nvidia B300 servers — the clearest sign yet that US chip controls are being routed around rather than obeyed.

sections.heading: Tencent Rents Its Way Around the Chip Fence
sections.body:
Tencent has signed a roughly $7 billion lease with Oracle to access about 100,000 advanced AI chips through data centers in Southeast Asia, according to reports from the Financial Times carried by Seeking Alpha and Yahoo Finance. The deal lets a Chinese hyperscaler rent compute physically located outside US jurisdiction rather than buying restricted accelerators directly.

The structure matters more than the headline number. By leasing capacity hosted in third countries, Tencent sidesteps the ownership and export path that US controls target. This is the same logic that a September Financial Times report flagged when it noted ByteDance gained access to more than 2,000 Nvidia B200 chips via a data center in Norway.

Washington's export controls were designed to stop advanced Nvidia silicon from reaching Chinese AI programs. A cloud-lease model turns that intent into a jurisdictional question — whose territory is the compute actually in — rather than a hardware-sales question.
sections.whyItMatters: If compute access can be leased from abroad, export controls on physical chip sales lose much of their bite. The frontier of enforcement is shifting from ports and customs to data-center contracts and cloud jurisdiction.

sections.heading: State-Backed Lender Financed Banned Nvidia B300 Servers
sections.body:
A Bloomberg report, relayed by CryptoBriefing, says a Chinese financing company controlled largely by local governments, Semi-Tech Leasing Group, helped bankroll purchases of Nvidia chips that the US has restricted from export. The hardware involved is Nvidia's Blackwell-series B300, a chip that sits directly inside the export-control fence.

The financing reportedly helped Glory View Technology acquire more than 700 servers, including machines running B300 chips. That a state-linked lender is the money behind the purchases suggests the flow of restricted hardware into China is not only smuggling by private brokers but embedded in provincial industrial policy.

This connects to a separate case announced this week: federal prosecutors in California charged Greg Lui, owner of Earthmade Computer, over a scheme to ship servers containing about $300 million of Nvidia chips to China between 2023 and 2024, routing them first through Malaysia and Singapore with falsified paperwork, according to Bloomberg via the Straits Times. Prosecutors cited a single purchase order for 27 servers with Nvidia H100 GPUs worth about $7.6 million. Lui faces conspiracy, smuggling and money-laundering counts carrying more than 20 years.
sections.whyItMatters: The pattern of state financing plus third-country routing plus private brokerage shows the export-control regime is being probed simultaneously from multiple directions. Enforcement is now a whack-a-mole game against a well-capitalized ecosystem, not a wall.

sections.heading: Beijing Weighs Letting ByteDance and Alibaba Buy Nvidia Again
sections.body:
Even as US controls tighten, Beijing appears to be loosening its own restrictions. According to The Information, relayed by Sedaily and Firstpost, China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has told firms including ByteDance and Alibaba that it plans to approve purchases of Nvidia's new RTX Pro 5500 chip, asking companies to report how many units they want and for what purpose.

The details cut against a simple 'China blocks Nvidia' narrative. The RTX Pro 5500 is a workstation chip carrying conventional GDDR7 graphics memory, not the high-bandwidth memory used in server-class AI accelerators — so it is a pragmatic stopgap, not a top-tier accelerator. Sources said ByteDance is weighing an order of about 1 million chips, with Nvidia reportedly planning to ship roughly 500,000 units per quarter to China starting in late December. The chip is said to sell for 85,000-90,000 yuan in China, close to the price of Huawei's Ascend 950PR.

Meanwhile, Huawei's rotating chairman claimed in late September that Huawei's homegrown AI chip sales now top Nvidia's inside China — a claim that, if true, is precisely what would push Beijing toward allowing some Nvidia imports to cover a domestic shortfall.
sections.whyItMatters: China is juggling industrial policy and performance. If Huawei's own silicon cannot close the gap, Beijing will import Nvidia selectively — weakening its sovereignty narrative but keeping its AI build-out moving.

sections.heading: Google's First Data-Center Satellite Reaches Orbit
sections.body:
On October 1, a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted 130 payloads to low Earth orbit on the Transporter-18 rideshare mission from Vandenberg Space Force Base, according to Space.com. The highest-profile payload was a pathfinder spacecraft for Project Suncatcher, Google's planned AI constellation.

The prototype is designed to test how Google's tensor processing units (TPUs) perform in space — specifically whether they survive radiation and whether the heat they generate can be dissipated efficiently. The same launch carried Cowboy Space's Reason-1 satellite, meant to prove out power beaming from orbit to a ground receiver, plus Starfish Space's first Otter servicing satellite.

Put together, these payloads show the private space sector pushing toward orbital compute and orbital logistics, not just imaging and communications. Google separately published research suggesting orbiting data centers are technically feasible.
sections.whyItMatters: If compute moves off-planet, the terrestrial grid, water and land constraints on AI data centers become one set of options among several. It is early and unproven, but the first hardware is now in orbit.

sections.heading: US Quantum Foundry Secures $1B CHIPS Award
sections.body:
Anderon, an IBM subsidiary, has finalized a $1 billion CHIPS and Science Act award with the US Commerce Department, converting a May letter of intent into a definitive agreement, per GovConWire. IBM is contributing a matching $1 billion in cash plus intellectual property, assets and workforce.

The company operates a 300-millimeter pure-play quantum wafer foundry in Albany, New York, and says the first quantum wafers are already running through the facility. It produces wafers for superconducting qubit arrays, quantum input/output signaling and readout signal-chain components, and plans to extend into other qubit modalities.

Commerce is taking a minority, non-controlling equity stake as a condition of the funding. The Anderon award is the largest of nine LOIs totaling $2.01 billion under the CHIPS Act's quantum portfolio, with GlobalFoundries separately finalizing a $375 million quantum foundry grant.
sections.whyItMatters: The US is now applying the CHIPS Act playbook to quantum — using equity-linked grants to seed domestic manufacturing in a technology that could define the next computing era. The state is a shareholder, not just a funder.

sections.heading: Europe Signals It May Slow the Huawei Rip-Out
sections.body:
European telecom operators may get more time to remove equipment from high-risk suppliers, as industry warns that an accelerated replacement could cost up to €40 billion and divert investment from fiber, 5G and future 6G networks, Reuters reports via TelecomLead.

The European Commission proposed in January 2026 that high-risk supplier equipment be phased out of critical sectors, originally with a 36-month deadline for mobile operators. But EU governments have removed that fixed deadline in proposed amendments dated September 22, replacing it with a timetable that weighs security risk, infrastructure lifecycles, replacement cycles, interoperability and availability of alternatives.

Deutsche Telekom CEO Timotheus Hottges and 16 other executives warned EU policymakers in September about the €40 billion figure. TelecomLead notes this is an industry estimate; other estimates are considerably lower. Germany, Italy and Spain face the largest replacement requirements.
sections.whyItMatters: Europe is discovering that security-driven de-risking has a price tag that competes directly with network investment. Allowing replacement to align with normal modernization cycles could blunt the policy's urgency — and ease pressure on Huawei without formally reversing course.

sections.heading: UK Is Europe's Most Targeted State-Cyber Victim
sections.body:
The United Kingdom now ranks as the most targeted country in Europe for nation-state and geopolitical cyber activity, facing 76 observed events in the past year, according to a new Microsoft report. The UK is also fifth globally for countries where customers are most frequently impacted by cyber threats, accounting for 3.8% of global activity.

Microsoft's data shows AI compressing the attack lifecycle — attackers can assemble sophisticated campaigns in minutes rather than days. Phishing jumped globally from 7% to 23% of incident-response intrusions year-over-year, and voice phishing climbed 502%. Ransomware detections rose sharply: 50% in the US, 276% in Germany and 66% in the UK. Research and academia was the most targeted sector at 38% of attacks against it, followed by transport at 22% and government at 13%.

Separately, South Africa has sought outside help after a cyberattack targeted its air traffic control agency, according to Dark Reading and South Africa's Sunday Times — a reminder that critical-transport systems in emerging economies are exposed alongside those in the West.
sections.whyItMatters: AI is lowering the cost of both attack and defense. The finding that entry points have barely changed — humans remain the weakest link — means the most sophisticated state actors still exploit basic vulnerabilities, and emerging-market infrastructure is increasingly in the crosshairs.

sections.heading: Türkiye Pushes AI and Data-Center Cooperation With Washington
sections.body:
Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır said Türkiye plans to deepen cooperation with the US in critical technologies including artificial intelligence and data centers, speaking at the fourth Turkish-American Business Meeting organized by ASKON during UN General Assembly week in New York, per Hürriyet Daily News.

Kacır credited dialogue between Presidents Erdoğan and Trump for opening strategic-sector opportunities and said bilateral trade had doubled over the past decade, though both sides target $100 billion. He cited more than 13,000 technology firms across 115 technoparks, over 1,700 R&D and design centers, and more than 310,000 R&D personnel. Annual exports exceed $280 billion, including $116 billion in medium-high and high-technology products.

On defense, Kacır said Türkiye aims to be one of the world's top 10 defense exporters by 2027, with domestic systems meeting more than 80% of the country's defense needs, and pledged to complete the Steel Dome air-defense system and extend the range of Turkish rockets and missiles.
sections.whyItMatters: Türkiye is positioning itself as both an AI investment destination and a defense-industrial exporter, leaning on US ties to attract tech capital. The pitch is sovereignty through partnership — building domestic capability while staying inside the Western supply chain.

bottomLine: The day's most consequential development was structural: Chinese firms are increasingly accessing advanced AI compute not by importing chips but by leasing them offshore (Tencent-Oracle, ~$7B for 100,000 chips) and by letting state-linked lenders finance banned hardware at home (Semi-Tech Leasing and Nvidia B300s). That two-pronged workaround — cloud jurisdiction abroad and state capital at home — suggests US export controls are being eroded faster than they can be enforced. At the same time the US deepened domestic capacity in a future technology, finalizing a $1B CHIPS award for IBM's quantum foundry, while Europe signaled it may slow its Huawei rip-out over a €40 billion cost estimate and the UK emerged as Europe's most targeted state-cyber victim. Expect the next battleground to be over cloud sovereignty and the legality of cross-border compute leases, not chip shipments.
sources: Seeking Alpha, Yahoo Finance, Financial Times (via Seeking Alpha/Yahoo), Bloomberg (via CryptoBriefing and Straits Times), The Information (via Sedaily and Firstpost), The Register, Space.com, GovConWire, TelecomLead, Reuters (via TelecomLead), Microsoft (via Yahoo Tech), Dark Reading, Sunday Times (South Africa), Hürriyet Daily News, Anadolu Agency
